beats.intro: Chapter eight, lesson 8. Allosteric Regulation and Feedback Inhibition. [[dial]]A thermostat does not heat a house forever. When the room is warm enough, it switches the heater off. When the room cools, it switches it back on. [[cells]]A cell has the same problem. Its chemistry runs all the time, and it must not make too much of anything. [[strip]]Here is our metabolic pathway again: a starting molecule, an enzyme at every step, and a product at the end. Today we light the stop sign that comes back from the product to the first enzyme.
beats.allo: [[chaos]]Without control, a cell's pathways would end in chemical chaos, with some products piling up and others running out. [[two]]A cell has two ways to prevent this. It can switch on or off the genes that encode specific enzymes. Or it can regulate the activity of enzymes it already has. Today is about the second way. [[site]]Allosteric regulation happens when a regulatory molecule binds to a protein at one site, and affects the protein's function at another site. [[both]]It may either inhibit or stimulate the enzyme's activity.
beats.switch: [[four]]Most allosterically regulated enzymes are made from several polypeptide subunits. Here is one with four. Each subunit has an active site, where the substrate binds, and a regulatory site, where an activator or an inhibitor binds. [[osc]]The whole enzyme swings back and forth between two forms, an active form and an inactive form. [[act]]An activator binds to a regulatory site and stabilizes the active form, so the enzyme keeps working. [[inh]]An inhibitor binds and stabilizes the inactive form, where the active sites no longer work, so the enzyme slows or stops. [[away]]Notice that the regulator does not sit in the active site. It binds somewhere else, and the change in shape does the work.
beats.q1: Quick check. For each statement, is it the active site, or the regulatory site?
beats.coop: [[prime]]Cooperativity is another type of allosteric activation. [[one]]A substrate molecule binds to the active site of one subunit. [[shape]]That binding stabilizes the active form of the whole enzyme, so the other active sites are ready. [[amp]]One substrate primes the enzyme to act on more substrate more readily, which amplifies its activity. It is allosteric because binding at one active site affects catalysis at a different active site.
beats.fb: [[line]]Now a real pathway. The initial substrate is threonine. Five enzymes in a line turn it into intermediates A, B, C and D, and then into isoleucine, the end product. [[e1]]Enzyme one, threonine deaminase, takes the first step. [[bind]]When isoleucine builds up, it binds to an allosteric site on enzyme one. [[off]]The active site can no longer convert threonine to intermediate A, and the pathway is switched off. [[use]]As the cell uses up isoleucine, it lets go. The active site is available again, and the pathway restarts. [[why]]This is feedback inhibition. The end product shuts down the pathway, so the cell does not waste chemical resources making more than it needs.
beats.q2: Quick check. What does isoleucine do to enzyme one?
beats.example: Let's follow the level of isoleucine. [[full]]Suppose the cell has plenty. Many isoleucine molecules bind to enzyme one, and it switches off. Little threonine is converted, so nothing is wasted. [[drain]]Now the cell builds proteins and uses isoleucine quickly. The level drops, the inhibitors let go, and enzyme one switches back on. [[swing]]So the level rises, falls and stays close to what the cell needs, just like a thermostat keeping a room steady.
beats.wrap: To sum up this lesson, and the chapter. [[recap]]Metabolism is a network of pathways. Energy flows downhill, A T P pays for uphill work, and an enzyme at every step lowers the activation energy. [[reg]]And cells regulate those enzymes. A regulator binds away from the active site and stabilizes the active or the inactive form. Cooperativity amplifies activity. Feedback inhibition lets the end product switch off its own pathway. [[end]]Now try the practice.
